content:
LAREDO — In Part I of this series, Webb Watch 956 read District 8 Council Member Alyssa Cigarroa's 30th-day campaign finance report and listed who is financing her run for mayor: $374,500 in total contributions between July 1 and September 24, 2026 (Cigarroa Campaign, 2026). This second part asks the follow-up question voters are entitled to ask about any candidate: what do the biggest names on that list have at stake in city government — and what power would a Mayor Cigarroa actually have over it?

Five family names carry the filing. Her own family gave $73,250. The Killam family and its companies gave $29,900. The Deutsch family gave $18,000. Evelyn A. Sames gave $10,000, Betty Bruni Moreno gave $10,000, and Alfonso Illan Arguindegui gave $5,000. Every dollar is legal and publicly disclosed — that disclosure is the only reason this article can exist. Nothing here alleges a deal, a promise, or a quid pro quo. What the public record does show, family by family, is documented city business: contracts, zones, boards and votes that run through the council a mayor presides over.

First, the rules of the game: what a Laredo mayor can actually do

Laredo's mayor is not a strong mayor. Under the city charter, all city power rests with the elected council; the mayor presides, is the city's official head, has no administrative duties, and "shall only vote in case of a tie of Council Members" (City of Laredo, 2006, §2.15). But read one section further and the office sharpens. Charter §2.07(C) requires five council votes — not four — for "levying of taxes, entering into contracts by the city, appropriating money from the City funds, granting any franchise or privilege… [or] conveying City lands," and it provides that when four council members vote yes, "this shall be deemed a tie and thus the Mayor votes" (City of Laredo, 2006, §2.07(C)). In plain terms: on contracts, taxes, appropriations, franchises and land — nearly every big decision in this article — a split council hands the decision to the mayor. Add a veto that takes five of eight council members to override, the power to call special meetings alone, and a direct nomination of one of the nine Planning & Zoning commissioners, whose terms run with the officials who nominate them (City of Laredo, 2006, §§2.07, 2.15, 9.02), and the picture is complete: a Laredo mayor rarely votes, but sits at the exact hinge of every contested contract and incentive the city signs. Tax-increment zone boards, like the one governing Killam's Winfield project, are appointed by the governing body that created them (Tex. Tax Code § 311.009), and economic-development incentives under Chapter 380 are acts of the council (Tex. Local Gov't Code § 380.001).

The Killams: $29,900, and the biggest land play in Laredo

The Killams are Laredo's largest private landholders — a fourth-generation family office founded on oil, now run day-to-day by third-generation David Killam (a $10,000 donor himself) and his sons Cliffe and D.W. (Texas Legislature, 2025). Their filing footprint is bigger than the three Killam-named entries — Killam Development LTD's $10,000, David Killam's $10,000, and $9,900 in billboard advertising donated in kind — because another $10,000 donor, Mary Lamar Leyendecker, is Cliffe Killam's mother, according to a Texas A&M International University endowment page (Texas A&M International University, 2024). She is also married to the head of a public-sector construction firm.

The family's documented city business starts with the single largest item in this investigation. On October 4, 2021, the City Council approved the amended ordinance creating Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone No. 2 — the Coves at Winfield: 1,027 acres at Loop 20 and Shiloh, planned for roughly 1,800 homes, 900 multifamily units, a retail town center, a hotel, and donated sites for Laredo College, a school, a fire station — and a hospital. Participating taxing entities committed 40% of their incremental tax value in the zone for up to roughly 30 years, against an estimated $77.1 million in public infrastructure Killam would build and recover through the zone (Virtual Builders Exchange, 2021). The project broke ground in June 2024 and is actively building out: by July 28, 2026, the Laredo Development Board heard its assessed value had climbed from about $11 million to about $60 million, that Killam had spent some $17 million — and that a prospective hospital parcel inside Winfield "could be over $100 million" (Citizen Portal, 2026). Cigarroa has sat on the council since 2020, so she was a member when the TIRZ 2 ordinance passed; the sources reviewed do not publish an individual roll call for that item, and Webb Watch will not assert how she voted until the official minutes are checked. What is not in doubt is the forward-looking math: Winfield needs years of plats, permits, utility extensions and possible TIRZ amendments, its board majority is appointed by the council (City of Laredo, 2006; Tex. Tax Code § 311.009), the family's two industrial parks are marketed on city water, sewer and "future extensions" of city roads (LoopNet, 2026), its retail tracts have needed rezoning flexibility, and its billboard business answers to a city sign ordinance. Every one of those decisions runs through the council chamber the mayor presides over — and, on a 4–4 split, through the mayor's own vote.

Her own family: $73,250, and one of the city's two hospitals

The largest bloc in the filing is the candidate's own name. The Cigarroa family gave $73,250 — roughly one of every five dollars raised — including $50,000 from Dr. Ricardo G. Cigarroa in two gifts of $25,000 (Cigarroa Campaign, 2026). Family funding of a family member's campaign is common and legal. The analytical point is the sector the family occupies. Dr. Ricardo G. Cigarroa runs the Cigarroa Heart and Vascular Institute inside Laredo Medical Center; his son and nephew practice there with him, and a federal court order in Doctors Hospital of Laredo v. Cigarroa described the family as four of Laredo's five interventional cardiologists before that antitrust case ended in summary judgment for the defendants in January 2025 (U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas, 2025). Webb Watch found no city contract held by the institute itself. The family's exposure is not a vendor contract — it is hospital policy, in a two-hospital city, at the exact moment the city is deciding the biggest hospital question in a generation.

The hospital file, start to finish

On June 24, 2024, the council voted unanimously — Cigarroa sitting as a member — to seek voter approval for a pediatric hospital, and sent the pricing to a Municipal Hospital Authority ad hoc committee (KGNS, 2024a). On November 14, 2024, the bond referendum's Health & Wellness Sub-Committee tabled the pediatric proposal and directed staff to get the positions of both hospital CEOs — Laredo Medical Center and Doctors Hospital — before proceeding (City of Laredo, 2024a). The children's hospital never made the May 2025 bond package (City of Laredo, n.d.). Meanwhile the private market moved into the same corridor: in May 2024, Clear Choice Health System's president pitched Webb County a $100 million-plus hospital at Loop 20 and Shiloh, explicitly seeking tax incentives (KGNS, 2024b) — and Clear Choice later bought a commercial tract inside Killam's Winfield (Citizen Portal, 2026). A $10,000 donor in Cigarroa's filing, Victor M. Vasquez, is very likely the same Clear Choice president; the identity match is probable but not confirmed, and Webb Watch flags it as such. This November, Proposition 1 asks voters, in an advisory measure only, whether the city should expand pediatric hospital services (Ballotpedia, 2026). And on September 21, 2026, it was Council Member Cigarroa's own agenda item — 26-C-154 — that contemplated a "funding mechanism to be adopted contingent upon voter approval" (City of Laredo, 2026b). The partner, the site and the financing are all still open — and all are council decisions a Mayor Cigarroa would preside over, champion, and, on a split vote, decide. The one route that competes with both hometown hospitals is also in motion: Driscoll Children's Hospital is scouting Loop 20 property for a Laredo clinic (KGNS, 2026).

So is it a conflict of interest? What the law actually says

Texas's recusal statute, Local Government Code Chapter 171, is narrower than the question. It requires an official to file an affidavit and abstain only when three gates all open: the official — or a relative in the first degree (parent, child, spouse) — holds a "substantial interest" in a specific business entity, meaning 10% ownership or income from that entity exceeding 10% of gross income; and the vote would have a "special economic effect" on that entity distinct from its effect on the public (Texas Legislature, 2009; Tex. Local Gov't Code § 171.002; Tex. Local Gov't Code § 171.004). Applied here, each gate is fact-dependent: public sources do not state Cigarroa's exact degree of kinship to each practicing Cigarroa physician; physicians practicing at a hospital are often independent rather than hospital employees, so the income test cannot be resolved from press coverage; and general policy — an advisory proposition, a funding mechanism of general application — usually fails the "special effect" test, while a contract naming a specific hospital partner is the paradigm case the statute was written for. Texas law also affirmatively shields an officer's legislative advocacy from sanction (Tex. Gov't Code § 572.059), and lawful, disclosed contributions are not bribes.

Laredo's own charter is stricter — on paper. Section 12.01 subjects every city officer to "the highest standards of conduct," forbids conduct that is "in conflict with or that has the appearance of a conflict with their duties," and makes a violation cause for forfeiture of office (City of Laredo, 2006, §12.01). That is the honest frame for the hospital file. Recusal law is built for council members voting on discrete items; it can cure a vote. It cannot reach the two years of agenda-setting, appointments, advocacy and partner-shaping that produce a deal's shape before any vote exists — and those are precisely the tools a mayor holds. Webb Watch located no Chapter 171 affidavit by Cigarroa concerning the hospital items in the sources reviewed; an affidavit may not have been legally required for those general-policy items, and the City Secretary's affidavit file — the authoritative record — is among the checks listed below. On today's public facts, this is not a clear-cut illegal conflict. It is squarely an appearance conflict under her own city's charter standard, and it is a legitimate thing for voters to weigh, stated exactly that way.

The fuel vendor: $5,000 in, $5.6 million a year in city business

The clearest vendor file of the five belongs to Arguindegui Oil. The city's own Legistar record shows the award of contract FY24-061 to Arguindegui Oil — up to $5,600,000 a year for unleaded and diesel fuel for the city fleet, chosen from six bids, on a two-year term with up to three one-year extensions that land squarely in the next mayor's term (City of Laredo, 2024b). A 2018 contract renewal and Webb County fuel bids show a long-running public-sector vendor, not a one-off (Webb County, 2020), and Transparency USA's Texas Ethics Commission data lists the company's president, $5,000 donor Alfonso Arguindegui, among the top contributors to the Laredo Political Action Committee as well (Transparency USA, 2026). Fuel awards are bid, and nothing here suggests the process was improper. The structural point stands on its own: the city's largest recurring commodity vendor has a direct financial interest in a friendly city hall, and its contract extensions will be approved by the council a Mayor Cigarroa presides over — and decided by her if that council splits 4–4.

The thinner files, stated plainly

Fairness requires saying where the trail is thin. Evelyn A. Sames ($10,000) is the fifth-generation head of Sames Auto Group, founded in 1910 and described as Texas's oldest dealership (National Automobile Dealers Association, 2025). Webb Watch documented exactly one piece of city business: Sames bought the naming rights to the city-owned arena in 2018 — it has been Sames Auto Arena since July 17, 2018 — and renewals of a naming deal on a city venue are council business (Wikipedia Contributors, 2026). State data also shows the family giving through the Laredo Political Action Committee (Transparency USA, 2026). No zoning case, incentive or fleet contract for Sames was documented. It is the thinnest file of the five, and it is presented that way.

Betty Bruni Moreno ($10,000) is thinner still. The filing entry reads "Moreno, Betty Bruni" — Bruni is her middle name — and while the wider Bruni family is an old Webb County ranching and oil name (the town of Bruni; a former Webb County Judge, Louis H. Bruni), Webb Watch found no documented city business involving this donor personally — no contract, zoning case, incentive or appointment — and her own business interests are not documented in reputable sources. (A different person, Sylvia Bruni, served on the 2024 bond sub-committee; that is not evidence about this donor.) Her contribution reads as establishment support, and anything stronger would be speculation. Webb Watch does not speculate.

What we still don't know — and what we asked

Five checks remain open, and this article will be updated as they close: (1) the official October 4, 2021 council minutes, for the TIRZ 2 roll call and how Council Member Cigarroa voted; (2) the City Secretary's Chapter 171 affidavit file, for any disclosure by Cigarroa on the hospital items; (3) the campaign's answer, requested on the record, to three questions it can settle in a sentence each — her exact kinship to the practicing Cigarroa physicians, whether she or first-degree relatives hold ownership in or draw more than 10% of income from Laredo Medical Center–connected entities, and whether she commits to a recusal protocol for hospital-partner decisions if elected; (4) the Killam family's prior-cycle giving, pulled directly from Texas Ethics Commission and city filings; and (5) confirmation of the Victor M. Vasquez identity flagged above.

The bottom line

A campaign finance report is not an accusation, and this article is not one. It is a map, drawn entirely from public records, of where a mayoral candidate's money comes from and where that money's interests intersect the powers of the office she seeks: a tax-increment zone and a possible nine-figure hospital parcel for the Killams; a fuel contract's extensions for Arguindegui Oil; an arena name for Sames; nothing documented for Bruni; and for her own family, the largest question in Laredo health care — a children's hospital whose funding, partner and site a Mayor Cigarroa would help decide, in a city where her family's name is on one of the two hospitals at the table. The law will police the votes. The charter asks voters to police the appearance. Both records are now in front of them.

excerpt: Alyssa Cigarroa's mayoral campaign raised $374,500, and five Laredo family names account for the biggest pieces of it. Webb Watch 956 traced each family's documented business with the City of Laredo — a tax-increment zone, a $5.6 million fuel contract, a hospital file — and read the charter and the ethics statute to answer a fair question: what can a mayor actually do for the people who financed her?
title: Follow the Money II: The Families Behind the Cigarroa Campaign — and What a Mayor Can Do for Them
